meta.title: Who really said "Shut up and calculate!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Feynman. Physicist N. David Mermin coined it in Physics Today, April 1989 — over a year after Feynman died. Sourced provenance and the misattribution trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Shut up and calculate!'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Feynman. N. David Mermin wrote it in Physics Today, April 1989, and in 2004 went looking for the Feynman source everyone cited. There wasn't one.

answer.label: Not Richard Feynman — actually N. David Mermin
answer.authorDates: b. 30 March 1935 · Horace White Professor of Physics Emeritus, Cornell University
answer.sourceLine: The line is Cornell physicist N. David Mermin’s, written in his Physics Today “Reference Frame” column for April 1989: if he had to sum up the Copenhagen interpretation in one sentence, it would be “Shut up and calculate!” Feynman had died in February 1988, more than a year before the column ran, and when Mermin went looking in 2004 for the Feynman source everyone cited, he found that not one of the sites crediting Feynman named a source ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Physics Today 42, no. 4 (1 April 1989), p. 9 — “Reference Frame” column

source.excerpt: If I were forced to sum up in one sentence what the Copenhagen interpretation says to me, it would be “Shut up and calculate!”
trail: 15 February 1988 — Richard Feynman dies. His Wikipedia biography gives 11 May 1918 – 15 February 1988 ↗, and makes no mention of this phrase.
April 1989 — more than a year later, Mermin’s Reference Frame column runs in Physics Today. Wikiquote sources the sentence to that column, page 9 ↗.

Early 2004 — Mermin reads a preprint calling the view “Feynman’s famous dictum”, fears he plagiarised it, searches his own back catalogue, and finds his 1989 column. He then searched the web and found that no site crediting Feynman gave a source ↗.

May 2004 onward — Mermin publishes the case that the phrase is his and invites anyone with evidence for Feynman to send it. Reference works now credit him: Wikipedia records that Mermin coined it and that it is often misattributed to Feynman ↗.
source.excerptNote: Mermin’s sentence from his April 1989 column, as he re-quoted it in his May 2004 Physics Today column while investigating why everyone was crediting Feynman.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in Physics Today in April 1989 — far later than the pre-1931 line for US public domain — so the column it comes from is in copyright, held by Mermin and his publisher; it was reprinted in his 2016 Cambridge collection Why Quark Rhymes with Pork. The four-word catchphrase circulates freely as a slogan, but the essay around it is not public domain.

author.name: N. David Mermin
author.heading: About N. David Mermin
author.metaLine: b. 1935 · American solid-state physicist · Cornell University
author.bio: N. David Mermin (born 30 March 1935 in New Haven, Connecticut) is Horace White Professor of Physics Emeritus at Cornell, where he joined the faculty in 1964. He is best known to students as half of Solid State Physics, the Ashcroft & Mermin textbook, and to physicists for the Hohenberg–Mermin–Wagner theorem and for importing the word boojum from Lewis Carroll into condensed-matter physics. He also wrote thirty “Reference Frame” columns for Physics Today between 1988 and 2009 — one of which produced the most famous sentence about quantum mechanics he never gets credit for.

cite.sourceCitation: N. David Mermin, “What’s Wrong with this Pillow?” Physics Today 42, no. 4 (April 1989): 9. Mermin set out the case that the phrase was his own, not Feynman’s, in “Could Feynman Have Said This?” Physics Today 57, no. 5 (May 2004): 10.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is one of the cleanest misattributions in physics: a living author, a dated publication, and a credited man who was already dead when the line appeared.

items.why: Feynman is credited on countless sites, T-shirts and even in the physics literature — Mermin first noticed the problem when a preprint called the view “Feynman’s famous dictum”. When he searched in 2004, Google returned more than 130 pages mentioning both Feynman and the phrase — about a dozen of which actually credited him — and not one of those cited a source or hinted at the circumstances ↗. Feynman died on 15 February 1988; the phrase was published in April 1989.

Feynman does have a famous line about the unintelligibility of quantum mechanics, and it gets blurred into this one: “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics” — The Character of Physical Law (1965), ch. 6, p. 129 ↗. That is an admission of bafflement, close to the opposite of an instruction to stop asking.

The phrase is often quoted as if it were Copenhagen’s own motto. It is not: it is Mermin’s outsider caricature of what Copenhagen said to him ↗, written by a physicist dissatisfied with that interpretation — and who later said he had come to hold a milder view of it.

misattribution.truthLine: The author is N. David Mermin, in “What’s Wrong with this Pillow?”, Physics Today, 1 April 1989 ↗ — and he only discovered the line was famous when he saw the credit going to somebody else.

context.heading: Why it stuck to the wrong man
lead: “Shut up and calculate!” is the four-word caricature of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics: stop asking what the wavefunction means, run the numbers, the numbers work. It is a real attitude with a real history — historian David Kaiser traces the pragmatic turn to wartime physics ↗ — but the slogan itself has a single, datable author, and he is not the man on the T-shirts.

Mermin coined it in April 1989 as self-deprecating shorthand for the advice his Harvard professors gave him when he asked awkward conceptual questions as a graduate student: stop being distracted by frivolities and produce some results. Fifteen years later he read a preprint describing the “shut up and calculate” view as Feynman’s famous dictum, briefly panicked that he had unconsciously plagiarised Feynman, went hunting for the source — and found there wasn’t one.
context.detailsSummary: The Matthew effect, and why Feynman is the last person who would have said it
detailsBody: Mermin diagnosed his own case using sociologist Robert K. Merton’s Matthew effect: scientific credit drifts to the most eminent plausible candidate. Asked who among the famous could have said something that irreverent, almost everyone lands on Feynman — Einstein, Schrödinger and Bohr are all obviously wrong for it. Being the only plausible candidate is not the same as being the author.

Mermin’s substantive objection is better than the missing citation. Feynman said he had always had great difficulty understanding the world view quantum mechanics represents, and that it still made him nervous — hardly the outlook of a man who tells the perplexed to stop asking. And nobody, Mermin noted, ever had cause to tell the best human calculator in physics to get on with the arithmetic.

Mermin has since distanced himself from the sentiment as well as reclaiming the words, describing his 1989 formulation as a brusque dismissal of a subtle position and saying he had come to hold a milder, more nuanced view of the Copenhagen interpretation.
context.pull: Nobody ever needed to tell Feynman to calculate.
